analysis.one_liner: Requires federally funded hospitals to offer emergency contraception to sexual assault survivors.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would require federally funded hospitals to offer emergency contraception to sexual assault survivors, was referred to committees and never received a vote in the 112th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have attached a condition to the Medicare and Medicaid money hospitals receive: to keep it, a hospital had to tell a woman who reports a sexual assault about emergency contraception, offer it to her, provide it to her at the hospital if she asks, and provide it even if she cannot pay. The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond committee referral in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are sexually assaulted and go to a hospital afterward. Under the bill, the hospital would have to tell them about emergency contraception, offer it, provide it on request without charge, and provide it even if the woman cannot pay—so survivors would not depend on whether the local hospital happens to offer it or whether a provider thinks to raise it. Hospitals would benefit from clear standards tied to their Medicare and Medicaid funding.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals receiving Medicare or Medicaid funds would have to promptly give sexual assault survivors accurate, unbiased information about emergency contraception, offer it to them, and provide it on request.
The services could not be denied because a woman or her family cannot pay.
The bill cites estimates that about 32,000 pregnancies result from rape each year, and that emergency contraception can prevent pregnancy if taken promptly.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals that receive Medicare and Medicaid funds would bear the cost of providing emergency contraception to sexual assault survivors without charge and of complying with the information requirements. Religiously affiliated hospitals that object to contraception would face the most direct conflict, since the funding condition would apply to them too. The federal government and taxpayers would bear no new direct cost beyond enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement mechanism is a condition on all Medicare and Medicaid funding, so any hospital that fails to provide emergency contraception to sexual assault survivors could jeopardize its federal funding—an approach critics could view as overly blunt, particularly for religiously affiliated hospitals that object to contraception.

The bill covers only survivors of sexual assault presenting at hospitals, not emergency contraception access generally, and relies on federal health care dollars as leverage rather than creating a direct right of action for patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—making sure a rape survivor is offered emergency contraception at the hospital where she seeks care—is significant and medically endorsed; the cost is modest (the drugs are inexpensive) and the mechanism (attaching conditions to Medicare/Medicaid funds) is a well-established enforcement tool. The main genuine objection is that conditioning federal funds creates a compliance burden for religiously affiliated hospitals that object to contraception, effectively requiring them to offer it or forgo federal health care dollars. The bill was designed narrowly around sexual assault victims rather than applying to all patients, which limits its scope.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees and their health subcommittees, and no markup or vote ever took place before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 4, 2011 and referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees.
Within two days it was referred further to subcommittees, including the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and no further action was recorded.
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill died without a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals that declined to offer emergency contraception kept full freedom to set their own policies, and no federal requirement was ever imposed. Rape survivors remained dependent on each hospital's individual practice.

for.name: 55 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 55 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, including its Health Subcommittee, and took no further action on it—no hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded.

sides.party_line_note: All 55 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never reached a floor vote, so the record shows sponsorship support only from one party and no recorded opposition votes.

industries.industry: Hospitals, including religiously affiliated hospital systems
industries.note: Hospitals would face a new condition on their Medicare and Medicaid funding: to keep it, they must offer emergency contraception to sexual assault survivors regardless of ability to pay. The bill's findings cite medical associations treating this as the standard of care, but it imposes a direct compliance mandate, felt most sharply by Catholic-affiliated hospitals.
The bill would create a guaranteed channel of provision for emergency contraception at hospitals, but with no new funding stream, so the financial effect is likely modest.
